findings.claim: The step 6 prerequisite probe checks that a USER token is refused on /admin/** but not that an ADMIN token is admitted, so the classic hasAuthority-for-hasRole slip in Task 2 gives a false role-row message about a correct row and no row names Task 2. Critic run at 505af8efafc0a91f276f379bf9f3a44da9dfb195, JDK 25.0.5, Maven 3.9.16 offline, on the private solution with only the chain's ADMIN rule written as hasAuthority("ADMIN") instead of hasRole("ADMIN") and the step 6 rows unchanged: the shipped converter maps the roles claim to ROLE_* authorities, so the ADMIN token holds ROLE_ADMIN and the rule (which compares the authority literally) refuses it. earlierTasks() sees the USER token refused on the unmapped admin path (403) and passes; the role row then sends the correct request (a customer asking for the admin statistics endpoint) and, as admin, gets 403 too, so it answers 'the role check did refuse this caller, but this API has no such admin action, so the row cannot show that an ADMIN may do it; aim at an admin action this API has'. That is false (the request targets the API's one admin action) and invites the learner to change a correct row; the other four rows pass, and README Troubleshooting line 194 promises that an unfinished earlier task is named first. Mitigation, hence low: it needs a deviation from the Task 2 TODO, which shows hasRole, and task2ProtectsEndpointsByPathAndRole ('expected:<200> but was:<403>' for the ADMIN user) and task4AcceptsItsOwnTokensAndRejectsTampering ('expected:<200> but was:<403>') fail in the same run with clear statuses.

Alternatively, in answeredByRoleCheck(), when the ADMIN request itself answers 403, name Task 2 instead of saying the API has no such action. Step 6 asks, for each of the five practices #o3 names, for the attacker request that practice is there to answer; the shipped check sends it against the running app and decides the row from the outcome. Critic acceptance sweep (a scratch-only subclass of SecurityLabTest calling the five shipped row checks reflectively on the solved app): 140 candidates (four callers times 30 method/path pairs, including case, slash, query, leading-zero and percent-encoded variants and both prerequisite probe paths, plus 20 login forms); no candidate passes two rows, neither probe path passes any row for any caller, and every accepted candidate is an instance of its own practice (a customer reaching the admin statistics endpoint; a login presenting the copied stored value for an existing account; a non-positive booking id with a token; a customer reading a booking of their own; a token-bearing request for a booking the caller cannot see or that does not exist). Practice-removal mutants with the solved rows unchanged each fail through their own row or prerequisite: raw password storage (hashing row names Task 1), the ADMIN rule removed (the prerequisite probe names Task 2 before any row runs), the @Positive constraint removed (validation row names step 3), the handler returning the Booking entity (DTO row names steps 2 and 3), ApiErrors emptied (safe-errors row names step 4), and a handler copying the exception message into its detail with one parameter, with an HttpServletRequest or with a WebRequest, and a fixed detail with the message in a problem property (each: safe-errors row 'the error body still reveals the exception'). So #o3 is practised by an executable learner act and checked behaviourally; the residual gap in the safe-errors leak probe for rarer handler shapes is recorded under cg-sme-apisec-020 and does not let a wrong practice-to-attack choice pass. The collapsed after-pass block names the OWASP risks; its statements match the live 2023 pages fetched this review (API2 'Is the API Vulnerable?': 'Uses plain text, non-encrypted, or weakly hashed passwords', https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa2-broken-authentication/ sha256 39896849743eb8bb01fede62bf479c6cd04e01e8b0d8a323a0ccf531ad6522fa; API5: 'Can a regular user access administrative endpoints?', https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa5-broken-function-level-authorization/ sha256 dc5f0056c015b0bca14fbaea14e79e777a97fdd46669c4c573bc4216cc439540; API3 'previously named: Excessive Data Exposure', https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa3-broken-object-property-level-authorization/ sha256 2643364bd8ff000b7cc3580c26e8487914361e10f546a6d8ec7abd4cc3972400; API8: 'Error messages include stack traces, or expose other sensitive information', https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa8-security-misconfiguration/ sha256 5017f8ca69871869697c75389c8cc017836d90ce1f067b24e21aa9a672ddf2fe; the 2023 list https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/ sha256 ac00589e1bb28f4977b3c82dfb61713b7aac0cbd07b15bd40d8516ef86379524 has no input-validation category; all retrieved 2026-11-19) and the topic page ('validation limits bad input; DTOs stop mass assignment and leaks; safe errors reveal less; hashing and role checks protect login and actions').

Narrowed but not closed. The leak probe (handlerEchoesExceptionText, lines 455-492) now invokes every @ExceptionHandler method that has a parameter matching the probe exception, filling ServletRequest, ServletResponse and WebRequest-type parameters and passing null for any other; it then catches any InvocationTargetException and skips that handler, and it inspects only String.valueOf of the return value, never the response it passed in. Critic runs at 505af8efafc0a91f276f379bf9f3a44da9dfb195 (JDK 25.0.5, Maven 3.9.16 offline), each changing only ApiErrors in the private solution: now caught, failing the row with 'the error body still reveals the exception': the loop-6 reproduction (detail copies the exception message, second parameter HttpServletRequest), the same with WebRequest, and a fixed detail plus a problem property holding the message. Still passing all 10 tests while the real body for Grace's request for booking 999 or Ada's booking 2 carries the service exception's text (critic body probe: the 404 detail repeats the service exception's own text, which names the booking id and the caller): (1) a handler whose second parameter is java.security.Principal and which reads the caller's name before copying the message (the probe passes null, the handler throws, the probe skips it); (2) a void handler with an HttpServletResponse parameter that writes a problem JSON with the copied message itself (the probe sees the null return). Both are supported @ExceptionHandler shapes in the live Spring Framework reference (https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/web/webmvc/mvc-controller/ann-exceptionhandler.html, sections 'Method Arguments' (mvc-ann-exceptionhandler-args: 'java.security.Principal - Currently authenticated user', jakarta.servlet.ServletResponse, Locale) and 'Return Values' (mvc-ann-exceptionhandler-return-values: 'A method with a void return type (or null return value) is considered to have fully handled the response if it also has a ServletResponse an OutputStream argument'), retrieved 2026-11-19T05:05:59Z, sha256 c6d82a20f6a21aeefe0a98436af10f113aec58d8e30b703cfda72b6caaefb2fe). So the ApiErrors TODO rule 'The detail must not repeat the exception message' is still not enforced for every supported handler shape. The common shapes are now covered and the residual ones are rarer, and the #o3 choice itself is unaffected (the learner still has to pick the safe-errors request), so the severity stays medium at most; the reconciler may lower it. Fix: drive the marker exception through the application's real exception resolution and read the written response (for example the context's handlerExceptionResolver bean resolving the marker against a MockHttpServletRequest with an authenticated principal and a MockHttpServletResponse for the booking path, then checking the response body for the marker), or at least pass a real Principal and Locale, treat a handler that throws during the probe as a failure rather than a pass, and check the probe response's content as well as the return value.

Critic probe test added only to a scratch copy of the solved work at 505af8efafc0a91f276f379bf9f3a44da9dfb195 (fresh Spring context, POST /auth/register over MockMvc): re-registering admin 409 with its stored hash unchanged and the admin login still 200; blank, empty and missing password 400 with nothing stored; missing and blank username 400; no body 400; a new name 201 then its login 200; that name again 409. Boundaries that remain and are now described accurately rather than overclaimed: in the running app the seeded booking owners are not accounts, so the first caller to register as ada can read Ada's booking 2 (probe: 201, then 200); and 201 versus 409 still tells an anonymous caller which names exist, which the live OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet ('Authentication Responses', https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html, retrieved 2026-11-19T05:06:00Z, sha256 e2b08fce883ce5a5277b6277f5e44adfc0b9b7e15b9a055e1739fc293d318a2d) lists as an incorrect account-creation response ('This user ID is already in use.'). The recommendation marked noting the enumeration signal as optional; neither boundary affects a test or a step 6 row, since the check registers through UserAccountService.
